title: Beyond Local Berry Geometry: A First-Principles Finite-Momentum Theory of Electronic Position
authors: M. S. Si, Y. Q. Li, G. P. Zhang
abstract: Electronic position controls how a crystal polarizes and responds to an external field. In crystals, it is usually described through local changes of electronic states in momentum space. This Berry framework has reshaped modern solid-state physics, but strong fields drive electrons across a finite momentum range, where coherence between different momenta becomes part of the response. Here we establish a first-principles theory of electronic position at finite momentum that retains this missing information. We show that unequal-momentum coherence can cancel under spatial averaging and still produce polarization, forming a coherence dipole. We obtain the matrix directly from material wave functions, without model bands or fitted transition elements. In Si, the finite-momentum geometry sets a material momentum scale. Comparing this scale with the momentum change driven by the field predicts when finite-momentum physics becomes active. Crossing the scale strongly reorganizes the fifth and higher harmonics, showing that momentum-space geometry, rather than emitted photon energy alone, controls the nonlinear response. HHG is the first demonstration, but the theory applies whenever driven electrons explore a finite momentum range. It therefore extends quantum geometry beyond the local Berry limit and provides a general basis for predicting field-driven phenomena in real materials.
summary: This paper presents a first-principles theory extending the concept of electronic position beyond local Berry curvature by incorporating finite momentum coherence. It shows that this unequal-momentum coherence forms a 'coherence dipole' that dictates nonlinear optical responses in materials under strong fields. The work provides a general, material-specific tool to predict field-driven quantum phenomena.
main_problem: To develop a first-principles theory of electronic position that accurately describes crystal response when electrons are driven across a finite momentum range, moving beyond the limitations of local Berry geometry.
main_result: The theory establishes that unequal-momentum coherence can form a 'coherence dipole,' which contributes to polarization even if it vanishes under spatial averaging. This shows that momentum-space geometry, rather than just photon energy, controls nonlinear optical responses like HHG.
method: The authors derive finite-momentum matrix elements using Bloch states and PAW wavefunctions, calculating contributions from both equal-$\mathbf{k}$ and unequal-$\mathbf{k}$ momenta to quantify the deviation from local theory.
model_or_system: The study concerns electronic structure in crystalline solids subjected to strong external fields. The theoretical framework uses a two-momentum construction applied to Bloch states defined on a finite Brillouin zone (BvK) domain.
key_observables: Electronic position, coherence dipole, Occupied-Subspace Distance ($	ext{Docc}(Q)$), and the geometric excursion ratio ($\chi_{	ext{geo}}$).
important_parameters: The material momentum scale ($Q_{10\%}^{	ext{geo}}$) compared to the field-driven momentum change ($\Delta k$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on specific definitions of the finite BvK domain and maintaining consistency across different coordinate branches during basis transformations.
figures_summary: Figure 3 illustrates $	ext{Docc}(Q)$ vs $Q$, showing recovery near $Q=0$ but systematic departure at larger separations, quantifying the crossover point $Q_{10\%}^{	ext{geo}}$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the failure of local Berry theory in strong fields, then developing the finite-momentum matrix element calculation using PAW methods, and finally demonstrating its physical relevance through comparisons to HHG phenomena.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous quantum geometric framework for understanding non-local response mechanisms in solids driven by intense fields, connecting fundamental electronic structure theory directly to observable nonlinear optics.
